message.content:
Below is a concise overview of the key rights and protections you have as a tenant in Texas. (This is general information and not legal advice; for specific situations you may want to consult an attorney or a local tenant‑rights organization.) | Area | What the law says | Practical Tips | |------|-------------------|----------------| | **Security Deposit** | • Landlords may charge up to one month’s rent for a furnished unit and two months for an unfurnished unit.
• The deposit must be returned within 30 days after you move out, minus any lawful deductions (e.g., unpaid rent, damage beyond normal wear). | • Get a written receipt and keep a copy of the lease.
• Take photos or videos of the unit before moving in and after moving out. | | **Habitability** | • Landlords must keep the premises in a safe, sanitary condition (e.g., functioning plumbing, heating, electrical, pest control).
• Texas law requires landlords to repair major defects that affect health or safety. | • Report problems in writing (email or letter) and keep copies.
• If repairs are not made within a reasonable time, you may withhold rent or pursue a repair‑and‑deduct remedy (see below). | | **Repair‑and‑Deduct** | • If the landlord fails to fix a major defect, you may pay for the repair yourself and deduct the cost from your rent, provided you give the landlord written notice and keep receipts. | • Keep receipts and document the defect.
• Notify the landlord in writing before making the repair. | | **Rent Increases** | • Texas has no statewide rent‑control limits.
• For month‑to‑month leases, landlords can raise rent at any time but must give at least 30 days’ written notice.
• For fixed‑term leases, rent can only be increased at the start of a new lease term. | • Review your lease for any rent‑increase clauses.
• Ask for a written notice if you’re on a month‑to‑month lease. | | **Eviction** | • Landlords must provide written notice: 3 days for nonpayment of rent, 30 days for lease termination (unless the lease specifies otherwise).
• For “no‑cause” evictions, a 30‑day notice is required.
• Eviction must be carried out through the court; landlords cannot forcibly remove you. | • Respond promptly to notices.
• If you believe the eviction is unlawful, you can file a “motion to stay” or “motion to dismiss” in court. | | **Privacy / Entry** | • Landlords must give at least 24 hours’ written notice before entering, except in emergencies.
• Entry is allowed for repairs, inspections, or showing the unit to prospective tenants or buyers. | • Keep a log of all entries.
• If you suspect unlawful entry, document the incident and consider filing a complaint. | | **Discrimination** | • Under the Texas Fair Housing Act and federal Fair Housing Act, landlords cannot discriminate based on race, color, religion, sex, national origin, disability, familial status, or source of income. | • Report discrimination to the Texas Commission on Human Rights or the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD). | | **Lease Termination** | • Either party can terminate a lease by giving proper notice (usually 30 days for month‑to‑month).
• Some leases include “early termination” clauses that allow you to break the lease for a fee. | • Read your lease carefully for any early‑termination fees or conditions. | | **Maintenance of Records** | • Landlords must keep records of rent payments and maintenance requests. | • Keep copies of all rent receipts, lease agreements, and correspondence. | | **Legal Remedies** | • If a landlord violates your rights, you can file a complaint with the Texas Attorney General’s Office, the Texas Commission on Human Rights, or HUD.
• You may also sue for damages or seek a court order to compel repairs. | • Document everything.
• Consider mediation or small‑claims court for disputes. | ### Quick Checklist for Tenants 1. **Read Your Lease** – Understand the terms, notice periods, and any special clauses. 2. **Document Everything** – Photos, videos, written notices, and receipts. 3. **Know the Notice Requirements** – 24‑hour notice for entry, 30‑day notice for rent increases or lease termination. 4. **Report Problems Promptly** – In writing, keep copies. 5. **Keep Records of Rent Payments** – Receipts, bank statements, or online payment confirmations. 6. **Know When to Seek Legal Help** – Unlawful eviction, discrimination, or persistent maintenance issues. --- #### Resources | Resource | What it Offers | How to Access | |----------|----------------|---------------| | **Texas Attorney General – Consumer Protection Division** | Consumer complaints, legal guidance | https://www.texasattorneygeneral.gov/consumer-protection | | **Texas Commission on Human Rights** | Discrimination complaints | https://www.tchra.org/ | | **U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD)** | Fair Housing complaints | https://www.hud.gov/ | | **Texas Small Claims Court** | Resolve disputes up to $20,000 | Local county clerk’s office | | **Local Tenant‑Rights Organizations** | Free legal clinics, workshops | Search online for “tenant rights Texas” | --- **Bottom line:** As a Texas tenant, you have the right to a habitable home, fair treatment, privacy, and protection against discrimination. If a landlord violates these rights, you have several avenues for recourse, from written notices to legal action. Always keep thorough records and seek professional advice when needed.
